newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW/ Disney TV benefits from switch.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW/ Disney TV benefits from switch.

text.p: The Disney Channel has been grabbing more viewers going the basic cable route, a switch from its origins as a premium - or pay - programming service, and momentum is likely to build, network President Anne Sweeney said.

"The response we're getting from the MSOs (multiple system operators) is overwhelming positive on the basic side," Sweeney said in an interview. "There's a lot of momentum in the marketplace. We expect that momentum will continue."
Charlie Nooney, senior vice president of sales and affiliate marketing, said, "Most of the growth is coming from the basic area."

The network, a unit of Walt Disney Co, tallied 30.1 million subscribers last month, with 25.2 million via basic service. In January 1995, the network had 13.1 million subscribers, with 7.3 million basic and 5.8 million as pay customers. The network first offered itself as basic in 1991.
Sweeney, at the helm since March 1996, declined to forecast subscriber growth. The company doesn't disclose data on revenues or profit for the channel.
Analysts estimated annual revenues at more than $300 million last year, and expect results to rise from the switch, as the channel gets more per-subscriber fees.

Asked if she saw the channel becoming 100 percent basic within a year or two, Sweeney said, "We don't know when that day will come. It may come eventually. (But) it could be that a percentage of our business is always going to be pay."

Nooney said the strategy among top operators -- including Tele-Communications Inc, the largest in the U.S.; Time Warner Inc ; Cox Communications Inc ; and U S West Media Group -- is to offer it as basic.
One big conversion would be Time Warner's giant cable system in New York City, the largest in the U.S., with more than one million subscribers.
Asked whether that system will switch, Nooney said, "We're always talking to them, but it's very hard to say."
A spokeswoman for the Time system said, "There have been discussions," adding, "There's not been a decision made yet."

One advantage of a basic network is the opportunity to sell advertising. Sweeney said it's not in the cards. There is "no plan right now" to carry advertising on the channel," she said. "It's not been something we created a plan for here."

As Disney shifts, Sweeney has changed the programming strategy. While premium channels are predominantly movies, she said, schedules for basic networks like USA, owned by Viacom Inc and Seagram Co Ltd ; and A&E (Disney, private Hearst Corp and General Electric Co's NBC) are "more toward consistent strip programming."

Sweeney found after conducting market research that much family TV watching was concentrated at 7 p.m. -- when dinner and homework were done. The network has programmed a daily Disney movie at that hour.
The Sunday movie will be dropped this fall when sister network ABC begins to offer its own Disney movie at that hour.

Did the corporate parent apply pressure? "It's something we decided to do," Sweeney said. "We asked: 'What's the biggest win for the company?' A movie versus a movie didn't seem ultimately to be smart for either one of us."
"That franchise has worked enormously well for us," she said. "We've seen better than steady growth. It has pretty significant viewing in primetime."
However, the channel will get first showings of all Disney animated "classics."
"We are the world premiere of animated classics," he said. The animated "The Hunchback of Notre Dame" will premiere next March.
The network has especially targeted nine to 11-year-olds, where the network has been battered by such as competitors as Viacom Inc's Nickelodeon network.
Disney said 9-11 viewership has jumped 117 percent versus a year ago, measuring the whole day.

Its so-called "middle-age kids zone" will offer such new programming as "Bug Juice," a documentary-like show about "real kids" at a Maine camp, and "Dinosaurs," a live-action sitcom about a domesticated dinosaur family.
